title: Will AOC Run for President?
author: Youth Outsider Editorial Team
dek: Socialists are drafting her, volunteers are signing up and the polls are split. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she will decide now that the midterms are over.
cover_alt: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez waving to a crowd at a 2025 rally

figures.alt: A Democratic Socialists of America rally in Milwaukee, June 2026
Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at a 2025 rally in Arizona

body:
On Saturday, the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America voted 291 to 123 for a resolution titled "Run AOC 2028 To Win A Democratic Socialist President," [Newsweek reported](https://newsweek.com/aoc-files-reelection-socialists-push-run-president-12725680). It is not a formal endorsement, but it commits the 15,000-member chapter to urging Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president and to building the groundwork for a campaign. Chapters in Los Angeles, Chicago, Ithaca and Wichita have passed similar resolutions, and DSA's national leadership has approved a process that could produce an endorsement in early 2027, [according to Jacobin](https://jacobin.com/2026/10/dsa-ocasio-cortez-2028-presidential-campaign).

The push is not only coming from socialists. Five days earlier, progressive activists and union leaders launched "Ready for AOC," a campaign that hopes to recruit 10,000 volunteers and collect a million signatures asking her to run. *"Movements like this work when they're loud and early, long before the candidate says yes,"* the group's website says.

Ocasio-Cortez has not said yes. She has not said no either. She has also filed paperwork with the Federal Election Commission to seek a sixth term in the House, a routine step that keeps her options open but settles nothing.

Ocasio-Cortez, 37, represents parts of the Bronx and Queens. She was a bartender and organizer when she beat Rep. Joe Crowley, a 10-term incumbent and one of the most powerful Democrats in the House, in a 2018 primary that almost no one saw coming. She has since become one of the best-known members of Congress. In 2025, she and Sen. Bernie Sanders drew some of the biggest crowds in American politics on their tour against what they called oligarchy, and she raised a personal record of $9.6 million in the first three months of that year, mostly from small donors giving an average of $21. She rejoined DSA in August after her membership lapsed.

For most of this year, she has given the same answer. In August, she told ABC's *This Week* that she was focused on the midterms but "I haven't ruled out the possibility" of running for president, [Axios reported](https://www.axios.com/2026/08/09/aoc-2028-president-schumer-senate). In September, she told The New York Times she would decide after the midterms whether to run for president, run for the Senate or stay in the House. She said she was thinking about a run "personally," acknowledged "a lot of conversation about electability," and said she does not "shy away from those realities."

The midterms are now over, and she is still not saying. On Nov. 10, she declined to endorse Sen. Chuck Schumer's bid to keep leading Senate Democrats, saying the frustration behind calls for new leadership is "seen in a lot of places" but that the decision belongs to senators. Asked about 2028, she said voters "don't want" to hear about the next election and want Democrats to use the power they just won.

That Senate question is one of her real options. Schumer's own seat in New York is up in 2028, and Ocasio-Cortez has repeatedly declined to rule out challenging him in a primary. A Senate race would be a more conventional next step. A presidential run would be a much bigger gamble.

Her supporters say the gamble is worth it. Democrats just won the House and the Senate, and some of the biggest wins went to insurgents like Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed and Los Angeles's Nithya Raman. Ocasio-Cortez has pointed to those wins as proof of a generational shift, telling ABC that millennials are now "grown adults with mortgages and kids." Her backers argue that she can turn out young and working-class voters who skip elections, the way Zohran Mamdani did in New York City last year.

The polls do not settle the argument. An AtlasIntel survey in May had her narrowly leading the Democratic field. A New York Times/Siena poll in October had her fourth, at 6%, behind Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom and Pete Buttigieg, with 45% of voters undecided. An Economist/YouGov poll taken Nov. 9 to 11 had her fourth again, at 12%, behind Harris at 20%, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff at 15% and Newsom at 13%. On the betting site Polymarket, she had a 15% chance of winning the nomination as of Tuesday, behind Ossoff at 26%.

Her critics, including many Democrats, doubt that a democratic socialist can win a general election. They argue that a more moderate nominee would do better with independents and Republicans who are unhappy with Trump. *"It's going to be difficult for a progressive to get out of the primaries and to win the nomination,"* George Washington University political scientist Todd Belt told Newsweek. Ocasio-Cortez has raised the issue herself. In the Times interview, she questioned whether a Latina could be elected president, [CNN reported](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/09/22/politics/alexandria-ocasio-cortez-2028-decision).

There is also a crowded field. Harris, Newsom, Buttigieg, Ossoff, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer are all considered possible candidates, and some Democrats have floated El-Sayed as a progressive alternative if Ocasio-Cortez stays out. He has said he is "not running."

So will she run? The honest answer is that nobody outside her circle knows, and she has every reason to wait. The first primaries are more than a year away, and the longer she holds off, the longer she can watch the field, the polls and the movement building around her. What has changed is the pressure. A year ago, the question was whether Ocasio-Cortez wanted to run. Now thousands of people are organizing as if she already has.
